Adult female Tan bristlemouth attain a maximum standard length of approximately 7.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 7.5 centimeters], a modest size consistent with the diminutive body plan common among mesopelagic gonostomatids. This ultimate length is reached after a prolonged growth period in the cold, stable waters of the deep ocean, where metabolic rates are relatively low. Field collections from the North Atlantic indicate that individuals achieving this size are typically several years old, reflecting the slow growth trajectory imposed by the species' thermal environment. The length-weight relationship derived from preserved specimens suggests that a female of this maximal size corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of about 1.6 grams [Wwi = about 1.6 grams], a value that aligns closely with the predictions of a standard length-mass power function for this genus. This diminutive adult mass stands in contrast to the much larger sizes observed in epipelagic lanternfishes, highlighting the energetic constraints of life at depth.

Sexual maturation in Cyclothone pallida is marked by the attainment of a standard length of approximately 4.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.3 centimeters], at which point gonadal development becomes histologically evident. Females reaching this pubertal length exhibit a corresponding wet weight of roughly 0.31 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.31 grams], representing a substantial increase from the mass at which they entered the exogenously feeding larval stage. The onset of puberty appears to be tightly coupled with somatic growth rather than chronological age, as individuals from different thermal regimes mature at similar sizes despite variable growth rates. This size-based maturation threshold is common among teleosts with indeterminate growth and ensures that reproductive effort is initiated only after sufficient energy reserves have been accumulated. The length at puberty represents approximately 57 percent of the ultimate length, a proportion that falls within the typical range reported for other small mesopelagic fishes inhabiting similar deepwater environments.

The earliest life stages of Tan bristlemouth are characterized by an exceptionally small initial mass. Following egg fertilization and subsequent embryonic development, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight of approximately 0.000014 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000014 grams], a value derived from the volume of the spherical egg, which measures about 0.3 millimeters in diameter. This minuscule birth mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva during the brief period before first exogenous feeding. Compared to other mesopelagic species that produce larger, more yolk-rich eggs, the extremely small size of Cyclothone pallida neonates suggests a strategy of high fecundity offset by low per-offspring investment, an adaptation to the unpredictable food availability typical of the deep scattering layer. During the lecithotrophic phase, the prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk stores, and the timing of the transition to active feeding is critical for survival.

Reproductive output in this species is linked to the thermal conditions of its deepwater habitat. At a temperature of 4.2 °C [T = 4.2 °C], females produce approximately 900 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 900 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately 3 to 4 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 to 4 times per year]. This annual reproductive schedule results in a substantial yearly fecundity, ensuring that a sufficient number of offspring are released into the oligotrophic environment to offset the high larval mortality rates typical of planktonic early life stages. The reproductive rate is sustained by the cold temperatures, which slow metabolic demands and allow the allocation of resources to gamete production over an extended breeding period. These spawning events are likely timed to coincide with peaks in secondary productivity in the mesopelagic zone, thereby enhancing the probability of larval encounter with suitable prey items after the yolk-sac stage is complete.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Cyclothone pallida, observed under the cold thermal conditions of its natural habitat at 4.2 °C [T = 4.2 °C], is approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years]. This extended longevity is remarkable for such a small-bodied vertebrate and is a direct consequence of the profoundly slow metabolic rates induced by the persistently low temperatures of the mesopelagic realm. The lifespan far exceeds that of similarly sized epipelagic fishes, which typically live for one to three years, and instead approaches the longevity observed in deep-sea gadiforms and some bathyal macrourids. This life-history strategy, combining slow growth, late maturity, and a long reproductive window, reflects the stable but resource-limited environment in which the species has evolved. The trade-off between a long lifespan and a low instantaneous reproductive rate per unit time underscores the adaptive suite that allows Cyclothone pallida to persist as one of the most abundant vertebrates on the planet.
